articles.title: IA já ajuda a escolher roupa, comida e até namoro; VÍDEO explica riscos de terceirizar decisões para chatbots | G1
articles.standfirst: Estudo mostra que conselhos dados por inteligência artificial podem influenciar escolhas e que pessoas já recorrem a ferramentas como o ChatGPT para decisões pessoais. Especialista alerta para riscos de dependência, vieses e perda de autonomia.
articles.summary: Estudo mostra que conselhos dados por inteligência artificial podem influenciar escolhas e que pessoas já recorrem a ferramentas como o ChatGPT para decisões pessoais. Especialista alerta para riscos de dependência, vieses e perda de autonomia.
articles.body:
“Essa roupa ficou boa em mim? Devo comprar?”, “devo pedir pizza ou hambúrguer?”, “o que eu respondo para a minha mãe?” ou até “devo terminar meu relacionamento?”.

Você já se pegou em dúvida sobre algo e foi pedir conselhos de vida para um chatbot de inteligência artificial (IA)? Que ela está cada vez mais presente no trabalho não é novidade, mas pesquisas mostram que a tecnologia tem sido mais usada (e mais convincente) para tomar decisões sobre nossa vida pessoal.

Um estudo de 2024 publicado na revista científica "Scientific Reports" e conduzido por Shinnosuke Ikeda, da Universidade de Kanazawa, no Japão, investigou até que ponto os conselhos do ChatGPT são capazes de alterar decisões humanas.

Em dois experimentos online com 1.925 participantes japoneses, pesquisadores compararam o efeito de orientações atribuídas ao chatbot com recomendações atribuídas a especialistas humanos.

Os resultados mostraram que, em determinadas situações, os conselhos da IA conseguiram influenciar decisões de forma semelhante aos atribuídos a especialistas. Os experimentos envolveram de dilemas morais a escolhas econômicas. A pesquisa também mostrou que pessoas com mais dificuldade e insegurança para tomar decisões eram mais suscetíveis às recomendações.

Em entrevista ao g1 , Cleber Zanchettin, professor de Enegenharia da Computação da Universidade Federal de Pernambuco (UFPE) e especialista em IA, explica que quanto mais as decisões são delegadas para a IA, mais a ferramenta conhece quem está perguntando e mais suscetível aos "conselhos" do chatbot essa pessoa fica.

“Quanto mais o usuário delega essas decisões, mais dados o sistema vai ter sobre você. Quanto mais dados o sistema tem sobre você, mais convincente vai ser a personalização que ele vai conseguir construir. E quanto mais convincente essa personalização, maior vai ser a capacidade de ele moldar as preferências e o comportamento”, descreve.

E dentro desse ciclo, o usuário pode acabar preso a essa "terceirização" de decisões.

“Na medida em que você não toma decisão, no futuro vai ficar esperando alguém tomar por você. Então, você se torna mais dependente da tecnologia”, diz.

Quando a IA é usada para a escolha de produtos a serem comprados, os riscos aumentam. Além da possível dependência, Zanchettin explica que as informações podem ser enviesadas.

Isso porque os modelos por trás dos chatbots "aprendem" sobre os produtos com base em conteúdos sobre eles na internet, o que inclui avaliações de outras pessoas que compraram e até as informações dos fornecedores.

A IA não testa o produto, e sim baseia a indicação no conteúdo que existe sobre ele na internet.

Então é melhor parar de pedir ajuda para a IA? Não necessariamente.

Zanchettin defende que as ferramentas podem ser úteis justamente para organizar grandes quantidades de informação e apresentar alternativas. A diferença está em usar a IA como apoio, e não entregar a ela a decisão final.

Na prática, em vez de pedir simplesmente que a IA escolha qual celular comprar, por exemplo, o usuário pode solicitar uma comparação entre modelos, prós e contras e diferentes alternativas — e decidir a partir dessas informações.

“Usar ela para dar opções e ponderar sobre essas opções. E, assim, você tomar uma decisão mais rápida e mais assistida, e não necessariamente ela tomar a decisão por você.”

articles.title: Cervejaria de Jundiaí conquista ouro com bebida inspirada na ferrovia | G1
articles.standfirst: Best Bitter da AHTRIO homenageia a história ferroviária e a influência inglesa na cidade. Cerveja Pilsen também foi premiada no Brasil Beer Cup 2026, competição que reuniu mais de 2,5 mil rótulos de 16 países.
articles.summary: Uma cervejaria de Jundiaí (SP) conquistou duas medalhas de ouro no Brasil Beer Cup 2026 e ficou entre as 50 melhores do Brasil. Uma das bebidas homenageia a história da ferrovia.
articles.body:
Uma cervejaria de Jundiaí (SP) conquistou duas medalhas de ouro no Brasil Beer Cup 2026, uma das principais competições cervejeiras da América Latina, e ficou entre as 50 melhores cervejarias do Brasil. Um dos rótulos homenageia as ferrovias e a influência inglesa na cidade .

A bebida produzida pela AHTRIO, no estilo Best Bitter, ganhou o primeiro lugar na categoria Special Bitter ou Best Bitter (cerveja amarga especial).

O g1 conversou com os sócios-proprietários do estabelecimento, Wander Lepre e Fernando Galvani, que explicaram as características das cervejas premiadas e o trabalho desenvolvido nas duas receitas.

Cervejaria de Jundiaí (SP) conquista ouro com duas cervejas diferentes no Brasil Beer Cup 2026 — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Sobre a Best Bitter, segundo Galvani, a ideia surgiu durante o Mês do Patrimônio.

“A nossa cervejaria sempre homenageia os patrimônios da nossa cidade, temos muitas raízes em Jundiaí. A cerveja tem um estilo inglês que homenageia o Espaço Expressa (complexo cultural instalado nas antigas oficinas da Fepasa) e toda essa parte das ferrovias, que foram construídas pelos ingleses”, explica.

Fernando Galvani, sócio-proprietário da Cervejaria AHTRIO, em Jundiaí (SP) — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

O fato da Best Bitter ser uma cerveja originária do Reino Unido facilitou a associação com a memória das ferrovias em Jundiaí, iniciada pelos ingleses da São Paulo Railway em 1867 e cuja arquitetura também está presente no antigo Complexo Fepasa, datado de 1892.

"A gente quis fazer a combinação dessa cerveja com a ferrovia, que foi trazida para cá pelos ingleses e teve toda uma questão de desenvolvimento aqui da nossa região”, acrescenta Wander.

AHTRIO Pilsen e AHTRIO Best Bitter, cervejas de Jundiaí (SP) premiadas com medalhas de ouro no Brasil Beer Cup 2026 — Foto: AHTRIO/Divulgação

A ATHRIO também foi premiada como a melhor cerveja pilsen, coroando um trabalho de mais de um ano de aperfeiçoamento da receita . O trabalho envolveu mudanças no processo e na própria receita, com o objetivo de manter a qualidade da bebida.

“Estamos muito felizes com o resultado porque vem coroar o trabalho de mais de um ano de evolução no nosso processo, evolução na receita, o carinho que a gente veio tratando essa receita, sempre com o intuito de entregar a melhor pilsen para os nossos clientes”, diz Fernando.

Wander Lepre, sócio-proprietário da Cervejaria AHTRIO, em Jundiaí (SP) — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

“Ganhar essa competição foi como um reconhecimento técnico da qualidade do trabalho que estamos desenvolvendo aqui em Jundiaí. Mais do que uma premiação, enxergamos essas medalhas como uma validação do trabalho de toda a equipe e da evolução da AHTRIO enquanto cervejaria", complementa Wander.

Wander destaca que a pilsen é o estilo normalmente mais produzido nas cervejarias e um dos mais consumidos pelos brasileiros. Segundo ele, apesar da aparente simplicidade, a produção exige atenção, porque pequenas variações podem alterar o resultado final.

“Essa produção é muito delicada, porque qualquer variação pode fazer com que a gente não entregue no final o que deseja. Então foi um trabalho árduo, mas essa medalha de ouro veio coroar realmente que nossas cervejas têm qualidade e que a gente faz isso com muito carinho”, afirma.

Cervejaria de Jundiaí (SP) conquista duas medalhas de ouro em competição internacional — Foto: Divulgação

A edição de 2026 do Brasil Beer Cup recebeu mais de 2,5 mil rótulos de 16 países. As cervejas foram avaliadas às cegas por mais de 100 jurados nacionais e internacionais entre os dias 7 e 10 de setembro, no Hotel Sesc Cacupé, em Florianópolis (SC). A cerimônia de premiação ocorreu no dia 12.

"Participar do Brasil Beer Cup já foi uma experiência muito importante. Ganhar as medalhas foi aquele tipo de reconhecimento que mostra que todo o trabalho que existe por trás de cada copo está no caminho certo. Tem muita dedicação, estudo, cuidado com o processo e, principalmente, uma equipe que leva cerveja muito a sério", finaliza Wander.

Antigas oficinas da Fepasa, em Jundiaí (SP), sediam o Espaço Expressa — Foto: Divulgação / Prefeitura de Jundiaí

AHTRIO Pilsen : leve e refrescante, tem coloração dourada, aroma de nobres lúpulos alemães e sabor equilibrado entre o suave dulçor do malte e um amargor firme, porém limpo e agradável. A cerveja tem 4,7% de teor alcoólico e 18 IBUs de amargor e, segundo a cervejaria, busca traduzir a tradição do estilo Pilsen, um dos mais consumidos no país;

AHTRIO Best Bitter : de coloração acobreada e brilhante, apresenta aroma intenso de malte, com notas de caramelo. A cerveja tem 4,6% de teor alcoólico e 40 IBUs de amargor, com sabor dos maltes especiais contribuindo para o equilíbrio da bebida.

🔎 "IBU" (sigla em inglês para International Bitterness Units, ou Unidade Internacional de Amargor) é a escala padrão usada para medir o nível de amargor de uma cerveja.

articles.title: As técnicas de recuperação pós-treino comprovadas pela ciência, e as que são apenas moda | G1
articles.standfirst: Embora muitos produtos prometam uma recuperação mais rápida, redução da dor muscular e melhor desempenho, a ciência costuma apresentar nuances mais complexas
articles.summary: Embora muitos produtos prometam uma recuperação mais rápida, redução da dor muscular e melhor desempenho, a ciência costuma apresentar nuances mais complexas
articles.body:
Concluir um treino intenso sempre dá uma sensação boa. Pelo menos até algumas horas depois, quando aquelas dores musculares incômodas começam a aparecer. Esse desconforto pode durar dias – transformando tarefas simples do dia a dia em um desafio.

Em busca de alívio, alguns frequentadores amadores de academias estão adotando o tipo de técnicas de recuperação antes reservadas aos atletas de elite. As redes sociais e o esporte profissional ajudaram a popularizar de tudo, desde banhos de gelo e roupas de compressão até massagens e suplementos de recuperação.

Embora muitos desses produtos prometam uma recuperação mais rápida, redução da dor muscular e melhor desempenho, a ciência costuma apresentar nuances mais complexas.

Poucas estratégias de recuperação receberam tanta atenção quanto os banhos de gelo. Isso envolve imergir em água a uma temperatura inferior a 15°C para acelerar a recuperação. Mas as evidências de benefícios são contraditórias.

Os banhos de gelo ajudam a aliviar a inflamação, o que pesquisas sugerem que pode reduzir a dor muscular e ajudar os atletas a recuperar a função muscular de forma mais eficaz em um período de 24 horas.

Mas há um porém. Embora a inflamação cause dor, ela também desencadeia adaptações que desenvolvem os músculos. Suprimir essa resposta com banhos de gelo pode limitar alguns dos benefícios a longo prazo do treinamento – especialmente se forem usados regularmente.

Quando se trata de banhos de gelo, evitar a dor a curto prazo pode comprometer os ganhos a longo prazo. É melhor usá-los apenas quando uma recuperação rápida for essencial.

As roupas de compressão são comumente usadas após exercícios para acelerar a recuperação. A ideia é que a pressão externa que elas aplicam favoreça a circulação, aumente o fluxo sanguíneo para os músculos e reduza o inchaço.

Mas, embora as roupas de compressão possam dar a impressão de que estão ajudando ao reduzir a dor muscular, as evidências de que elas realmente melhoram a recuperação muscular são, em geral, menos convincentes.

Um estudo de 2022 as colocou à prova. Um grupo recebeu roupas de compressão; o outro grupo recebeu um comprimido de placebo, sobre o qual foi informado que era tão eficaz quanto a compressão.

Comprovou-se que as roupas de compressão melhoram a circulação e o fluxo sanguíneo muscular, enquanto o placebo não teve efeito sobre esses indicadores. Isso sugere que os efeitos das roupas de compressão na recuperação são fisiológicos e não se devem simplesmente à expectativa ou à percepção.

Mas não está claro se essas mudanças melhoram significativamente o desempenho. Embora evidências recentes sugiram que as roupas de compressão afetem genuinamente alguns indicadores de recuperação, é improvável que elas restaurem diretamente a função muscular.

Portanto, as roupas de compressão podem ajudar principalmente porque fazem com que você se sinta mais recuperado.

A massagem é uma das poucas intervenções de recuperação com suporte científico relativamente consistente. Ela pode reduzir a dor muscular e melhorar a percepção de recuperação após o exercício.

Atualmente, não está claro quais mecanismos realmente desencadeiam os benefícios da massagem para a recuperação. Isso pode se dever ao fato de que a massagem reduz a rigidez muscular, melhora a circulação e promove o relaxamento.

Mas embora os atletas sintam menos dores e a percepção de recuperação melhore após uma massagem, as medidas objetivas de desempenho e função muscular são modestas e inconsistentes.

A massagem pode aliviar o desconforto do treinamento, mas não espere uma recuperação milagrosa do desempenho.

O mercado de suplementos nutricionais é um grande negócio, com centenas de bebidas e cápsulas em cores vivas que prometem redução da dor muscular e recuperação mais rápida. Mas nem todos os suplementos são iguais. Alguns parecem trazer pequenos benefícios, enquanto outros vêm acompanhados de promessas exageradas que a ciência não comprova.

A proteína de soro de leite, por exemplo, é um suplemento bem estudado. Rica em aminoácidos (os blocos de construção das proteínas), ela estimula a síntese de proteínas musculares – o processo que ajuda seus músculos a crescerem. A proteína de soro de leite demonstrou ter benefícios de pequenos a moderados para a recuperação muscular – mas as evidências de que ela possa aliviar a dor muscular são inconsistentes.

Os aminoácidos de cadeia ramificada (BCAAs) são suplementos amplamente utilizados que geralmente contêm uma mistura dos aminoácidos leucina, isoleucina e valina. Os BCAAs são populares porque acredita-se que a leucina que contêm estimule a síntese proteica.

No entanto, apesar de sua popularidade, os BCAAs parecem menos eficazes do que fontes completas de proteína para a recuperação muscular. Isso ocorre porque a reparação muscular requer todos os aminoácidos essenciais – não apenas aqueles encontrados nos BCAAs. Fontes alimentares como frango, carne bovina, salmão e tofu contêm todos os aminoácidos essenciais.

O suco de cereja ácida é um suplemento relativamente novo no mundo do fitness. É rico em polifenóis – compostos vegetais que, segundo se diz, têm efeitos anti-inflamatórios e antioxidantes (reduzindo ou prevenindo danos celulares). É por essas razões que se acredita que o suco de cereja ácida ajude a reduzir danos e dores musculares .

Embora essa ainda seja uma área emergente de pesquisa, as evidências sugerem que esses compostos tenham efeitos de pequenos a moderados na redução da dor muscular após os treinos e também possam ajudar a restaurar a força e a potência muscular.

Os suplementos de ômega-3 (óleo de peixe) são frequentemente recomendados como uma forma de reduzir a inflamação e acelerar a recuperação após o exercício. Embora algumas pesquisas sugiram que eles possam reduzir modestamente a dor muscular e ajudar a preservar a função muscular após exercícios extenuantes, os resultados estão longe de serem consistentes. Dessa forma, é improvável que os suplementos de ômega-3 melhorem significativamente a recuperação.

É importante ressaltar que todos esses nutrientes podem ser obtidos por meio de uma alimentação saudável e equilibrada. A ciência também mostra que é melhor obter esses nutrientes a partir de alimentos integrais do que de suplementos caros, pois os alimentos integrais fornecem outros nutrientes importantes que podem interagir sinergicamente para promover a saúde.

Técnicas populares de recuperação podem trazer pequenos benefícios para reduzir a sensação de dor muscular, mas, na verdade, não costumam restaurar a função muscular de forma significativa. Em vez disso, as evidências mais sólidas para uma boa recuperação vêm dos princípios básicos:

1. Priorize o sono: Durma 7 a 9 horas por noite para que o corpo possa realizar processos vitais de recuperação e adaptação.

2. Alimente-se adequadamente: Consuma 20g a 40g de proteína após o exercício para a reparação muscular e uma ingestão adequada de carboidratos para repor as reservas de energia.

3. Treine com inteligência: Combine um bom sono e uma boa alimentação com um plano de treinamento sensato e bem estruturado. Isso inclui reservar dias de descanso entre as sessões, desafiar-se um pouco mais a cada vez e programar sessões mais leves quando necessário para permitir a recuperação.

Portanto, talvez a maior lição aqui seja que a recuperação não pode ser engarrafada e vendida.

articles.title: No action but endless talks, is Mecca defence agreement a pact without an impact?
articles.summary: As Houthi missiles and drones continue to pound southern Saudi Arabia, a glaring question has emerged from the crisis: where is Pakistan?
articles.body: As Houthi missiles and drones continue to pound southern Saudi Arabia, a glaring question has emerged from the crisis: where is Pakistan? More than a month after Islamabad signed a landmark mutual defence pact with Riyadh, its much-publicised commitment to the kingdom's security appears to exist only on paper.On August 7, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA), a pact explicitly stating that an armed attack on any one of the three nations would be treated as an attack on all. Framed as a NATO's Article-5 style collective security arrangement, it was meant to signal a new era of coordinated deterrence among the three states.Yet since Iran-backed Houthi rebels intensified missile and drone strikes on Saudi cities including Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan, Najran and Taif, as well as a drone interception near the city of Mecca. These strikes have injured dozens of civilians and setting oil installations ablaze. The Houthi's have also launched unsuccessful strikes on Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh as well. Pakistan has been conspicuously silent on the ground. There has also not been a formal invocation of the collective response clause that Islamabad itself helped negotiate just weeks earlier.A press release from Saudi Arabia, dated April 11, 2026, states that Pakistani air force fighters and support aircraft have been deployed at the Abdulaziz Air Base in the kingdom's eastern sector. This airbase is close to Bahrain on the Persian Gulf. This deployment is in accordance with the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement signed between the two countries, as per the Saudi release. Meanwhile Pakistani media has put troop numbers at approximately 8,000, or a brigade level and a squadron of JF-17 Thunder fighters, which has been assembled in Pakistan. Two squadrons of military drones, and a Chinese-origin HQ-9 long-range air defence system. Crucially, all this equipment is operated exclusively by Pakistani personnel, while Saudi Arabia foots the entire bill, covering deployment, operational and logistical costs, along with per-soldier compensation paid to Islamabad.Pakistan has boots, jets and air defence systems already stationed in Saudi Arabia, fully funded by Riyadh, and yet none of it has been visibly activated even as missiles rain down on Saudi soil and alerts have been sounded over the holy city of Mecca itself. The contrast between a paid, standing military presence and its complete absence from the current conflict has not gone unnoticed.Pakistan's inaction stands out further given its central role in two other Saudi-led security frameworks. The Islamic Military Counter Terrorism Coalition, a 43-nation alliance, has been commanded by former Pakistani army chief General Raheel Sharif since 2017, yet despite the Houthis being designated a terrorist organisation by Saudi Arabia and other states, the coalition has not been mobilised against the ongoing campaign. Pakistan also holds the deputy command of the newly formed Multinational Maritime Defense Coalition, set up specifically to counter Houthi threats to shipping in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb, yet here too, no visible operational response has followed.Although, on September 25th Turkish and Pakistani army chiefs held talks in Riyadh to discuss support for the Kingdom under the ambit of the MJDA, according to Saudi Arabia. The Turkish and Pakistani military chiefs agreed to deepen their military and intelligence cooperation and enhance the integration of defensive capabilities, as per the same document. The release stated that 'they reaffirmed their commitment to collective defence and the determination of the three countries to defend Saudi Arabia's security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity', but the document did not state how the Pakistanis and the Turks would strengthen the Kingdom's defence or an timelines to bring in any strong defensive capabilities. Just hours after the meeting Houthis launched missiles towards Khamis Mushait in Saudi Arabia, which were intercepted by Saudi air defences, even as the army chiefs of Pakistan and Turkey were in country.The pattern raises questions about the substance behind Pakistan's defence partnerships in the Gulf. Islamabad was quick to project the Mecca agreement as a major diplomatic and strategic win in August. But when Saudi Arabia has actually come under sustained attack, that momentum has not translated into action, so the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement for now seems to be a pact without an impact.

articles.title: Vancouver workers opened a shipping container of T-shirts and found 14 duffle bags holding 329kg of cocaine worth C$5.8 million; police say it is the city's largest-ever cocaine seizure
articles.summary: Vancouver workers expecting to find boxes of T-shirts inside a shipping container instead discovered 14 duffle bags containing 328.55 kg of cocaine worth
articles.body: Vancouver workers expecting to find boxes of T-shirts inside a shipping container instead discovered 14 duffle bags containing 328.55 kg of cocaine worth an estimated C$5.8 million, according to police. The seizure is the largest cocaine seizure in the history of the Vancouver Police Department.The drugs were discovered by employees at a legitimate Vancouver-based company while they were sorting through a shipment of T-shirts. Police said the company had ordered the clothing and had no connection to the cocaine found inside the shipment.The employees discovered the drugs and immediately contacted police. Officers were called to the business on July 21, where they seized the cocaine concealed in 14 duffle bags.“Obviously, the business was shocked by what it found. They called police right away and are in no way associated with the seized cocaine,” Sgt. Travis Fraser said in a statement.Police said the quantity of cocaine, along with stamps and packaging found with the drugs, suggests that the shipment was connected to organised crime. “This amount of drugs, as well as the stamps and packaging, clearly indicates organised crime is behind the shipment,” Fraser said.Investigators are now tracing the journey of the shipping container, which travelled through multiple countries before reaching Canada.According to police, the container left Honduras on May 18. It was then loaded onto a vessel and stopped in Jamaica on June 6. The shipment later arrived in Montreal on July 5 before eventually making its way to Vancouver.Police believe the cocaine was not supposed to reach the Vancouver company. Instead, investigators suspect the drugs were meant to be removed from the container somewhere along its journey before the shipment reached its final destination.“We believe the cocaine was supposed to be removed prior to its arrival at the company,” Fraser said. “For some reason, it was not unloaded.”The discovery has now triggered an international investigation involving authorities in several countries. Vancouver police said they are working with law enforcement agencies in Canada, Honduras, Jamaica and the United States as they try to determine who arranged the shipment and who was supposed to receive the cocaine. The investigation is also examining how the drugs were concealed among the legitimate T-shirt order and how they remained inside the container until it reached the Vancouver business.No arrests had been made at the time of the police announcement. Authorities have asked anyone with information about the shipment, the cocaine or the people involved to contact police.The seizure stands out not only because of the quantity of cocaine involved but also because of how it was discovered. Rather than being intercepted during a targeted operation, the drugs were found by employees who were simply unpacking a commercial shipment.For the Vancouver company, what appeared to be an ordinary T-shirt delivery unexpectedly became the centre of a major international drug investigation. Police are continuing to follow the shipment's route from Honduras through Jamaica and Canada as they work to identify those responsible.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Did Facebook help or hinder search for missing Corrie Mckeague?
articles.summary: Desperate for answers, the 23-year-old's mum used social media in an attempt to find him.
articles.body:
Desperate for answers after the disappearance of her son, Nicola Urquhart went online and set up a Find Corrie Facebook page - little did she know how big it would become.

RAF gunner Corrie Mckeague, 23, went missing on 24 September 2016, after wandering the streets of Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk, having been separated from his friends following a night of drinking.

The mystery surrounding his disappearance became a source of fascination, speculation and crowd-sourced detective work to online supporters who called themselves "Corrie's Army". The #FindCorrie hashtag frequently trended on Twitter and Nicola's Facebook page grew to 120,000 followers.

Ten years on, did social media help or hinder the search for Corrie?

The airman, who became a dad to daughter Ellie nine months after his disappearance, was officially declared dead in 2022, but his body has never been found.

After years of searching an inquest ruled he had died after climbing into a Biffa bin before it was tipped into a waste lorry.

Nicola, a former police sergeant, came to accept the ruling and eventually said the Suffolk Police had "got it right", after previously being critical of its handling of the investigation.

When she felt the force was not listening to her or taking her theories and suggestions seriously, she took to social media to put pressure on officers.

One Facebook post, next to a photograph of Nicola searching through woodland, was shared almost 270,000 times around the globe.

"We wouldn't have had the investigation we did without the support we had from local people and over 100,000 people giving me a loud voice," Nicola told the BBC.

"I would write a post on Facebook and the public would then get right behind it - there was a direct correlation between social media and the local people and [action].

"It probably made it very difficult for the police, but for us social media was fantastic, had a massive impact and it was so good for me as someone searching for their son."

In recent years, social media has become a common feature in high-profile cases of a missing people - notably the disappearance of 45-year-old Nicola Bulley in Lancashire in 2023.

In that case, police warned people against harmful speculation and "online abuse" . There were also fears the search area had become a tourist spot because of the social media profile.

The nature of social media has also grown and evolved. When Corrie disappeared Twitter had not yet been rebranded a X.

The platform that would eventually become TikTok – initially named Douyin - launched in China on 20 September 2016, four days before he went missing. Today the platform said it is used by more than 30 million people in the UK.

Facebook has about 58.5 million users in this country. Would this have changed anything in Corrie's case?

"It's difficult to answer because if it had happened 10 years later, Corrie would've been TikTok famous, without a shadow of a doubt," said Nicola.

"Not because he went missing, because he would have still been here and he would have just been TikTok famous – the world would've already have known Corrie.

"If we had all of the social media we have today, would it have been different? I don't know, because as a family we would've still behaved the same way."

While Nicola quickly became well-versed in utilising social media, she believes in 2016 the police were still "catching up" with how useful it could be to investigations.

She accused the force of issuing appeals for information on social platforms, but failing to respond to the public.

"They didn't expect the volume of calls to come in that did and people said they'd been in touch with social media at the police, but they were not answering," she said.

"So, it was a learning curve for them and they've had to adapt to social media and the impact it can have."

Suffolk Police said its thoughts were with Corrie's family and friends. It has closed the inquiry and said it would only reopen it if any "new, realistic and credible information becomes available".

Guidance published in February by the College of Policing said if a force does not have the capability to monitor social media responses 24-hours a day, it should record the risk of not doing so.

Forces should also have processes in place to manage surges in social media traffic.

After her son's disappearance, Nicola, who lives in Scotland, said she would be regularly contacted by other parents and families across the country asking for help to find their missing relatives.

For while, she obliged and did all she could to support them, again using social media to, in her view, force action.

On one occasion, she said she helped a family who wanted support with a search on Facebook to find a loved one.

"That's exactly what they did, and they found him. It didn't make me feel good because somebody died, but it made me feel relieved that they'd found him," she said.

But what could be the downsides of using social media to help search for a missing loved one?

According to a study by University College London, 68.5% of the 44,935 UK adults surveyed said they had experienced some kind of online abuse.

Nicola said her family's experience of using social media was "overwhelmingly positive", but there had also been some "truly horrific" moments and fabricated tip-offs.

"We had people phoning [the missing persons number], putting posts or leaving messages on my phone saying, 'Corrie is in my attic, I've got him tied up'," she said.

"We knew that was ridiculous and wasn't real, so some of the things we laughed about with dark humour because they were so ridiculous. But other things did hurt."

Matt Navara, a social media consultant, said online platforms can be a powerful way for families looking for a loved one to put a face in front of thousands of people and keep an appeal alive when news coverage might have moved on.

Yet, he added, it can also lead people to analyse footage without any context or turn up at a location because they have seen it in a video.

On 16 September, Corrie would have celebrated his 33rd birthday.

Nicola described him as being "so unforgettable" – something that, if the ongoing engagement on the Find Corrie Facebook page is anything to go by, has proved true.

"Generally, after about six months of somebody dying, people don't want to talk about that person because they don't want to make the person feel bad or sad," she added.

"But 10 years on, people we've never met are still asking how we are and talking to me about my son."

articles.title: Strictly Come Dancing: YouTube creator John Nellis to compete
articles.summary: The social media star from Newcastle, County Down has been paired with Katya Jones - but what do people in his hometown think?
articles.body:
Away from his day job of interviewing the likes of Erling Haaland and Kylian Mbappé, John Nellis has taken to a different discipline to showcase his talents.

The social media star, from Newcastle, County Down, has been paired with Katya Jones in this year's series of Strictly Come Dancing .

Nellis quit his job as an air traffic controller four years ago and is now flying high on social media as one of the UK's biggest sports content creators, with a combined audience of more than 20 million followers across social media.

BBC News NI has spoken to people in his hometown about how they feel about him Cha Cha Cha-ing across the famous Strictly dancefloor.

One of Anna Monteith's best friends is John's younger sister Fiona, so she has known him most of her life.

"He's one of the most genuine people that I know, he's bubbly, charismatic, he can talk to a room full of people and is the exact same person day and night," she said.

"It is all down to his family and his upbringing and it really shines through - when he's on stage or in his local for a pint."

Monteith added that she will be tuning in to the show, calling it "a milestone for him - it is a great inspiration to all the kids in the local area".

"To see someone go so far, which in the past may have been a dream to meet Ronaldo or Messi, to a young boy in a classroom that is inspiration enough, that could mean he will do his GCSEs or A-levels and will go on to do that and follow in the footsteps," she added.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, when most planes were grounded Nellis had more time to work on his hobby - making videos, which led to him becoming a full time content creator.

His football-focused YouTube channel has attracted 16 million subscribers and more than 11 billion views.

Alan Imrie is the event supervisor in the Anchor Bar in the Newcastle.

He first met Nellis playing football with Tullymore United and from in and around the town.

"It is unbelievable what he's done, from working in air traffic control to give it all up to just skyrocketing from there," he said.

"Anytime he comes in here he is just the same down-to-earth guy. He would always go out of his way for kids wanting photos."

Nellis is still involved in the community, Imrie explained.

"We had a charity game at Christmas there and he managed to get the likes of Shane Todd etc to play in it.

"He sponsors a lot of our youth, he's put a lot of money into our football club, which is unbelievable.

"Fame can change people, but John just goes out of the way to talk to anyone."

A former pupil at Shimna Integrated College from 2004-2011 Nellis even came back to the school as a lab technician in 2013.

The assistant vice-principal at the college is Joanne Poland and having taught Nellis GCSE science and A-level biology, Poland said it is not hard to remember teaching him.

"He was so friendly and one of those pupils that did speak to teachers, he was confident in himself and he liked a bit of craic.

"We have a programme every June where we get our former students to come back and talk to our students about their careers. I contacted John and he agreed to come back".

However all did not go to plan as the day before Manchester United had announced a big signing and had asked Nellis to do a video around it - but he still did a call in the midst of it all.

"It was an online call, in the airport and he was fantastic," said Poland.

She said it was good for the students to hear both the "challenges and opportunities" he had on the way to YouTube success.

Jack McMullin said Nellis's "content is class" and added that he will often call "in locally for a pint, you see him round the street and he's a lovely bloke to talk to".

"He's over meeting YouTubers in England and footballers, Haland and stuff - some achievement that you'd never expect from someone around here."

Grace Susay is a language teacher at Nellis's alma mater and said he has the "personality to engage different types of people and talk to people, which not everybody has".

Susay said his recent attention was "great for the local community to see somebody that they would know from around the town actively doing something and to be putting themselves out there".

What does she think of his chances of bringing home the Glitterball?

"I'm really looking forward to him doing some Latin dances," she added.

"As someone who teaches languages, if he can pull off the Salsa, the Paso [Doble] that would be fantastic - I could see him pulling that off."

Nellis will join the ranks of other celebs from Northern Ireland such as Gloria Hunniford and Christine Lampard who have appeared on the show before.

articles.title: Fuel costs putting off meal delivery driver applicants in Jersey
articles.summary: Maureen Bougeard says some prospective volunteers do not respond after learning about expenses.
articles.body:
A delivery service offering meals to people in need has spoken about the challenges of recruiting new volunteers due to rising fuel costs.

Maureen Bougeard said Meals on Wheels Jersey had received £38,000 from the Jersey Community Foundation to fund work supplying hot meals to islanders who are unable to prepare meals themselves.

She said the service packed and delivered meals to about 100 people, four days a week - but added fuel costs were having an impact.

"Very often volunteers say, you know, 'the petrol's getting expensive'," she said. "We're looking for new volunteers and I send the information out which says 'you drive your car at your own expense' and I don't hear from them again."

The secretary said the organisation had more than 200 volunteers.

"Our complete organisation is run by volunteers," Bougeard said. "We don't have any paid staff at all."

Bougeard said some of the voluntary meal delivery drivers drove the length of the island twice in a day, adding most volunteers were retired people.

"I'm not saying everyone has a poor pension, not everyone is on the basic pension, but some are and they still manage to come and volunteer, which is absolutely fabulous," she said.

The service said people who receive the meals currently pay a cost price of £5.

It said the grant from Jersey Community Foundation covered the charge to the government of Jersey's health and community services, which supply and facilitate the preparation of the meals. The service said the grant had been offered for 2026 and 2027.

Meals on Wheels said it hoped to renegotiate the service level agreement with the government to allow it to continue.

articles.title: Shailene Woodley joined scientists in the Sargasso Sea to collect microplastics; why this remote Atlantic ecosystem became a real-world pollution laboratory
articles.summary: Far from the beaches and busy coastlines where plastic pollution is easiest to see, scientists found evidence of a much less visible problem in the
articles.body: Far from the beaches and busy coastlines where plastic pollution is easiest to see, scientists found evidence of a much less visible problem in the Sargasso Sea. During a 2019 Greenpeace expedition, actress Shailene Woodley joined researchers collecting samples from the remote North Atlantic ecosystem, where floating Sargassum provides habitat for marine life. As reported by Greenpeace, one sample contained 1,298 microplastic fragments, highlighting how tiny pieces of plastic can accumulate even in distant ocean waters. The findings placed the Sargasso Sea within a wider debate about marine pollution, while Woodley's involvement connected the scientific expedition with a campaign for stronger protection of international waters.The Sargasso Sea became the focus of a scientific expeditionWoodley joined Greenpeace on an expedition to the Sargasso Sea in 2019, travelling with scientists who were collecting samples for microplastic research. The location mattered because the Sargasso Sea is a remote open-ocean ecosystem rather than a heavily developed coastal environment.The Sargasso Sea is an area of the North Atlantic defined by ocean currents rather than a physical shoreline. Those currents help concentrate floating material in particular parts of the ocean. Plastic that has broken down into progressively smaller pieces can remain in the water column and move with these circulation patterns, allowing researchers to examine pollution far from the places where much of the original material was used and discarded.That made the expedition useful for a broader question. If plastic fragments could be detected in such an isolated marine environment, the problem could not be understood simply as a matter of litter washing up on a beach.The plastic pollution hidden beneath apparently clean waterThe material being collected was not the sort of plastic waste that can be picked up by hand. Microplastics are generally tiny fragments or particles produced when larger plastic items break apart, although some are manufactured at small sizes. Their scale changes the way pollution behaves in the sea. Larger objects can sometimes be tracked, removed or photographed. Much smaller fragments can become dispersed through seawater and interact with marine organisms in ways that are considerably harder to see.The Sargasso Sea therefore offered researchers a place to examine a form of pollution that can be present without creating an obvious visual sign. A stretch of blue water can appear clean while containing thousands of minute plastic particles.That contrast is part of what made the expedition scientifically useful. The absence of visible rubbish did not necessarily mean the absence of plastic.One Sargasso Sea sample contained 1,298 microplastic fragmentsDuring the Greenpeace expedition, scientists recorded high concentrations of microplastic in the North Atlantic. One sample contained 1,298 microplastic fragments, a figure reported as exceeding levels found in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.The comparison is striking because the Sargasso Sea is not normally associated with the enormous accumulation of floating debris that has made the Pacific region famous. Yet the sampling showed that significant concentrations of tiny plastic particles could exist in another remote ocean system.A single sample cannot describe every part of the Atlantic, and concentrations can vary considerably depending on currents, location, depth and sampling conditions. What the expedition provided was a snapshot of pollution within an ecosystem that is otherwise difficult to observe from land.A remote ecosystem is also a nursery for marine lifeThe Sargasso Sea has another reason for attracting scientific attention. Its floating mats of Sargassum provide habitat in the open ocean, where shelter can be limited.The ecosystem is associated with juvenile sea turtles and other marine organisms that use the floating vegetation as habitat and feeding grounds. The relationship between plastic pollution and these organisms is therefore an important part of the wider research question.Microplastics do not remain neatly separated from marine ecosystems. Small particles can be encountered by organisms at different levels of the food web. Understanding exactly what happens after exposure is complex and depends on the species, the type of plastic, the concentration and other environmental conditions.For scientists working in the Sargasso Sea, the issue is consequently larger than measuring plastic alone. The samples provide evidence about what is present in the water within a living ocean environment.The Sargasso Sea expedition became part of a bigger campaignWoodley's involvement brought a recognisable public figure into a scientific campaign, but she had concerns about celebrity environmentalism before agreeing to take part.She wanted to know what Greenpeace intended to do with the expedition and how the information gathered at sea would feed into wider action. Her position, as described by National Geographic, was that taking part only made sense if the work extended beyond a photograph or a social media post.That approach became part of her longer involvement with Greenpeace's campaign for stronger protection of international waters. The Sargasso Sea expedition was connected to the organisation's work around the High Seas Treaty, an agreement intended to create a legal framework for conserving marine areas outside national jurisdiction.Woodley later took part in advocacy aimed at policymakers and United Nations officials, rather than treating the expedition as a standalone environmental appearance.The pollution story reaches far beyond the Sargasso SeaThe significance of the expedition lies partly in what it says about the geography of plastic pollution. Plastic entering the ocean does not necessarily remain close to the source. Currents can transport floating material over considerable distances, while sunlight, waves and physical abrasion can gradually break larger objects into smaller fragments.That creates a difficult research problem. By the time a scientist finds a microplastic particle in an offshore sample, its original source may be impossible to identify. The Sargasso Sea offers an unusually clear example of this problem. It is geographically remote, yet it is connected to the wider Atlantic circulation system. The plastic found there is part of a much larger movement of material through the ocean.A laboratory without wallsCalling the Sargasso Sea a pollution laboratory does not mean it is an artificial testing site. It is the opposite. The value comes from studying pollution under real ocean conditions, within an ecosystem shaped by currents, floating vegetation and marine life.Scientists can collect water samples, count particles and identify the types of plastic present. Those measurements can then be considered alongside information about the area's currents and biology.The work also illustrates why microplastic research often begins with something as simple as a water sample. Much of the problem cannot be understood from photographs of beaches or large pieces of floating rubbish. The smaller material requires sampling and laboratory analysis. In the Sargasso Sea, the ocean itself becomes the study environment.Woodley's ocean work continued after the expeditionThe 2019 expedition was one part of a wider period of environmental campaigning for Woodley. Her involvement with ocean issues later included public advocacy for the High Seas Treaty and appearances connected with marine conservation.As reported by Sustainable Fisheries UW, she also appeared in the 2024 PBS documentary series Hope in the Water, in an episode examining overfishing and alternatives to conventional seafood. The programme looked at ways seafood production and consumption could place different pressures on marine ecosystems.Her environmental work has not been limited to the ocean. Before turning more heavily towards marine conservation, Woodley became involved in grassroots organising around the Dakota Access Pipeline protests in 2016. She had also worked on voter canvassing in rural California, experiences that introduced her to organisers working outside the entertainment industry.The Sargasso Sea expedition sits within that longer pattern. The setting was remote, the pollution was largely invisible, and the scientific work depended on gathering evidence rather than simply documenting what could be seen from shore.Why the Sargasso Sea matters to microplastic researchThe expedition offered a useful reminder that marine plastic pollution is not confined to crowded coastlines or recognisable garbage patches. Tiny fragments can occur in remote parts of the Atlantic, including waters that support distinctive ecosystems.For scientists, the Sargasso Sea provides a place to examine that problem within the ocean itself. The samples collected there help reveal what is present beneath an apparently clean surface, while the surrounding biology raises questions about how persistent plastic particles interact with marine life. That is what turned the remote Atlantic region into a pollution laboratory. The sea did not need to be covered in visible rubbish for researchers to find evidence of human waste. The particles were already dispersed through the water, small enough to be missed by the naked eye but measurable when scientists went looking for them.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Inside Trump-Xi’s high-stakes meeting
articles.body:
A red-carpet welcome, ceremonial honours, high-stakes talks and a carefully watched handshake: Donald Trump and Xi Jinping’s meeting brought the world’s two biggest economies into focus. As the US and Chinese leaders met in Washington, trade, technology, Taiwan and global tensions shaped the conversation.

Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington for his first visit to the US capital in more than a decade, setting the stage for a closely watched summit with Donald Trump. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump personally welcomed Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan at Joint Base Andrews, with a red-carpet reception, military band and ceremonial honours marking the start of the high-profile visit.

The ceremonial welcome continued at the White House, where Trump hosted Xi with military honours and a formal review.

Trade was among the biggest issues hanging over the summit. Ahead of the leaders' meeting, US and Chinese officials agreed to extend their existing trade truce, which had been due to expire in November. The extension was intended to prevent another immediate escalation in tariffs, but it did not resolve the deeper trade disputes between Washington and Beijing.

Trump and Xi also exchanged symbolic gifts.

Trump presented Xi Jinping with a bald eagle representing America.

Xi also added a softer touch to the summit by announcing that two giant pandas would soon head to Atlanta.

'US very happy,' says President Donald Trump

Trump said the visit was a positive development for both countries and indicated he was open to accepting Xi’s invitation to visit China in the future.

The summit also featured a lavish state dinner hosted by Trump and Melania Trump, adding ceremony to the high-stakes diplomatic engagement. The reception was part of a broader effort to project warmth and stability in the relationship. Yet the pageantry came alongside unresolved disagreements over trade, AI, Taiwan and wider geopolitical tensions between the two countries.

The meeting ended with both leaders emphasising the importance of the relationship, but there was no clear breakthrough on the biggest strategic disagreements. The trade truce was extended, while questions surrounding other geopolitical and global issuesremained. The summit nevertheless provided an opportunity for Washington and Beijing to keep dialogue open and manage tensions between the two competing powers.

articles.title: In 1985, a 10-year-old threw a message bottle into the Atlantic; 37 years later, a Florida family found it and mailed his childhood note back to him
articles.summary: In a touching tale of nostalgia and ocean magic, a Kentucky man receives his long-lost childhood note after it was discovered in a bottle washed ashore by Hurricane Nicole. The story highlights the enduring connection between children’s dreams and the vastness of the ocean.
articles.body: For generations, kids on beach vacations have tried the same straightforward experiment. Half expecting the sea to take their words to some far stranger, they scribble a little letter, fold it inside a bottle, and hurl it into the waves. Most of these bottles are lost at sea, buried in sand, or broken against rocks. Occasionally, however, a child's note reappears decades later and reaches someone who has long forgotten who wrote it. That's precisely what happened to a Kentucky man whose message drifted in the Atlantic for 37 years before a family on the Florida coast found it and traced it back to him.A childhood note sealed in glassIt was 1985, and ten-year-old Troy Heller was on a family holiday in Vero Beach on the Atlantic coast of Florida. He wanted to attempt something he had never done before. He scribbled a brief letter, asking whoever found it to call or write him, included his contact details, put the paper in an old glass Pepsi bottle and tossed it into the sea. It was the kind of modest, hopeful gesture most children make and then forget about. Heller was no exception. He grew up and resided in Mount Washington, Ky, and never gave the bottle another thought.Way before satellites, government scientists used this precise kind of sealed bottle to investigate how water travelled over the oceans, a procedure with a remarkably deep institutional history. Agencies in the United States have cast thousands of drift bottles into the sea since the eighteenth century, requesting finders to report the date and site of discovery so researchers may chart ocean circulation, as the NOAA Ocean Service has detailed in its archives. Some of those scientific bottles floated back up after decades at sea, a chronology not far different from what Heller’s personal note would eventually undergo.The storm brings the past ashoreThe bottle’s reappearance coincided with one of the more odd weather phenomena of 2022. That November, Hurricane Nicole hit the coast near Vero Beach, another uncommon late season storm, and only the third hurricane on record to strike the US mainland in November, after the 1935 Yankee Hurricane and 1985's Hurricane Kate. Beaches all along Florida's eastern coast, including parts badly ravaged weeks earlier by Hurricane Ian, churned up in the storm and dislodged all manner of long-buried debris.Heller's bottle was among the objects that came ashore, recovered on a beach near Sebastian, Florida, about 13 miles north of where it was first tossed. The Carrmax family discovered it while helping to remove storm debris. They opened the bottle and found a legible note with a phone number attached, then set out on a quest to track down its author. Their investigation took them right to Heller in Kentucky, who was shocked to be shown evidence of something he had done as a boy and never expected to hear about again.Most message bottles are never recovered at all, lost to the sea long before anyone finds them. It counts as a statistical rarity, not a common occurrence: a glass bottle that survives nearly four decades of tides, storms and salt water, only to be found by people determined to track down a stranger a thousand miles away.Today’s floating bottles and the quiet scienceHeller’s account is somewhere between folklore and a very real branch of oceanography that’s still going on now, just with far more powerful instruments. Researchers no longer use glass vials for this kind of work. Instead, they use satellite-monitored buoys that work on the same basic idea but automatically communicate their position, delivering real-time information to weather and climate models. Today, NOAA’s Global Drifter Program has more than a thousand of these buoys drifting around the world’s oceans at any given moment, and the data they produce helps forecasters understand everything from surface currents to the behaviour of storms like Nicole.His bottle was never going to be a scientific instrument but a child's secret hope that someone, somewhere, would read his words. But it travelled the same secret routes that buoys and research vessels take every day, showing in the most personal way imaginable exactly how far and how long the ocean can carry something little. Nearly forty years later that same interest came back to him, brought home by a hurricane and a family of strangers who thought to look a little harder at what the storm had left behind.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kosovo is preparing to remove its first dam; the Mirusha project aims to reconnect 35 kilometres of river habitat
articles.summary: Kosovo is preparing to remove the obsolete Mirusha Dam, opening up 35 kilometres of river habitat and restoring free-flowing conditions along a river that
articles.body: Kosovo is preparing to remove the obsolete Mirusha Dam, opening up 35 kilometres of river habitat and restoring free-flowing conditions along a river that ecological surveys have identified as a biodiversity hotspot. The Mirusha River flows through an area of high ecological and landscape value and is connected downstream to the Mirusha Waterfalls Nature Monument, a nationally protected area that depends on the river's natural flow regime. According to the Open Rivers Programme, which is funding the demolition project with local organisation Ecopana, surveys recorded 157 animal species in the river, including 83 aquatic species. The project is expected to reconnect approximately 113 kilometres of river habitat in total when tributaries are included, consisting of 35 kilometres upstream of the dam and 78 kilometres downstream. The removal is scheduled to take place between September 2026 and January 2027 and is intended to restore natural flow and sediment transport, improve water quality and allow fish to move through habitat currently blocked by the dam.The dam was built without required permits in 2009The Mirusha Dam is an approximately 9-metre-high reinforced-concrete structure built by the Municipality of Malisheva in 2009 without the required environmental and water-management permits, according to the Open Rivers Programme. The organisation describes the barrier as obsolete because it does not generate hydropower, provide drinking-water supplies or deliver essential irrigation services, while its current recreational use is limited. Technical investigations identified cracks, damaged spillway elements and other structural deficiencies. During flooding in January 2026, the structure had to be partially opened because of increased water pressure, which the project documentation identifies as highlighting safety risks associated with the deteriorating dam. The structure also fragments river habitat and alters the natural movement of water and sediment. According to the project documentation, stagnant conditions upstream have allowed untreated wastewater and organic pollution to accumulate, contributing to the river's poor ecological condition. Complete removal is intended to address both the ecological fragmentation and the risks associated with the ageing structure.Ecological surveys found a spider species new to scienceThe biodiversity surveys carried out around the Mirusha River also contributed to the discovery of a spider species that was previously unknown to science. In a study published in Zootaxa titled Description of a new Eratigena Bolzern, Burckhardt & Hänggi, 2013 (Arachnida: Araneae: Agelenidae) from the Balkans based on an integrative approach, researchers formally described Eratigena mirusha, a spider from Kosovo, using morphological and molecular evidence. The species is now recognised as endemic to Kosovo, with the World Spider Catalogue listing its distribution as Kosovo. The Open Rivers Programme identifies Eratigena mirusha among the species associated with the Mirusha biodiversity hotspot and says the species was identified with support from an earlier Open Rivers Programme grant. The dam-removal project lists Chondrostoma ochridanum, Pachychilon pictum, Rodeus amarus, Rhyacophila macedonica and Eratigena mirusha as focal species. The Albanian roach, Pachychilon pictum, is classified as Near Threatened, while Rodeus amarus is the species currently listed by the project for the European bitterling.Removing the dam should restore natural flow and sediment movementThe project is designed to remove the entire vertical extent of the Mirusha Dam rather than modify the existing structure. According to the Open Rivers Programme, the removal is expected to restore natural flow and sediment transport, enable fish movement, improve water quality and support the recovery of aquatic biodiversity and river morphology. The organisation also says that the dam currently contributes to stagnant conditions in which untreated wastewater and organic pollution accumulate upstream. These changes are intended outcomes of the project rather than results that have already been observed, since demolition has not yet taken place. Monitoring will therefore be carried out before, during and after removal to record changes in water quality, macroinvertebrate communities, fish communities, sediment dynamics and the physical form of the river. The distinction is important because the project's ecological benefits are projections based on the planned restoration intervention, not measurements of conditions after the dam has already been removed.The removal builds on Kosovo's first dam-removal projectThe demolition follows an earlier Open Rivers Programme pre-demolition grant that funded preparatory work for removing the barrier. The organisation describes the current project as Kosovo's first dam-removal demonstration project and says it is intended to strengthen institutional knowledge and provide a practical model for future river-restoration initiatives in the country. The demolition timeline is September 2026 to January 2027, meaning the project is still forthcoming rather than completed. It forms part of a wider European river-restoration effort by the Open Rivers Programme. In an August 2026 announcement, the programme said it was supporting 33 new projects across Europe and that its overall portfolio had reached 243 projects in 35 European countries. It also reported that projects supported by the programme had removed 141 barriers and reconnected 1,820 kilometres of river. The Mirusha project therefore represents both a local restoration effort and part of a broader attempt to reconnect fragmented river systems across Europe, with its results to be assessed through the monitoring programme once removal begins.You use AI every day. articles.title: $30bn tariff cut, Iran and AI dialogue: Key points from Xi-Trump talks
articles.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping wrapped up his three-day state visit to Washington on Friday, announcing that he will meet US President Donald Trump twice
articles.body: Chinese President Xi Jinping wrapped up his three-day state visit to Washington on Friday, announcing that he will meet US President Donald Trump twice more before the end of the year, taking the total number of face-to-face meetings between the leaders of the world’s two largest economies in 2026 to four.The visit focused on strengthening the US-China relationship, with the two sides reaching agreements and setting up mechanisms covering trade, investment, energy, drug trafficking, critical minerals and emerging technologies. Trump and Xi also discussed global issues including the war in Iran, while agreeing to maintain dialogue and pursue a relationship based on strategic stability, respect, fairness and reciprocity.The visit was criticised by some in the US as heavy on ceremony but light on substantive breakthroughs, with no major progress announced on issues including trade or the safety of artificial intelligence. The two leaders, however, sought to project continuity in their efforts to preserve a stable relationship and agreed to continue discussions on several areas in the months ahead.The state visit, which concluded on September 25, marked the first visit by a Chinese president to the White House in more than a decade.$30 billion tariff reduction frameworkThe two countries operationalised the US-China Board of Trade and the US-China Board of Investment, which were established after the May 2026 summit in Beijing.Under the Board of Trade, the two sides reached consensus on recommendations for more favourable tariff treatment for $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction. The board also launched a working group on market access barriers in agriculture.US exports covered under the recommendations include agricultural goods, fish and seafood, logs and wood products, cosmetics and medical devices, while US imports include consumer products such as small appliances, toys, holiday decorations and children’s car seats.China will also import at least 10 million metric tons of US coal in 2027 and again in 2028.The Board of Investment will provide a government-to-government channel to discuss investment opportunities and investment-related barriers. Separately, the two countries agreed to continue work on US concerns over supply shortages involving rare earths and other critical minerals, with the aim of restoring shipments to appropriate levels.China and the US had already been working on a reciprocal tariff reduction framework covering $30 billion worth of products from each side.Focus on drugs and energyThe United States welcomed China’s scheduling of orphines, a class of deadly drugs, and noted China’s new export controls on two fentanyl precursor chemicals. Washington also encouraged the permanent scheduling of these and other substances and chemicals to curb the flow of illicit precursors to drug producers in North America.The United States said that, acting on information from US law enforcement, China arrested 21 Chinese citizens in August 2026 for the manufacture and distribution of precursor chemicals to illicit drug producers in North America. The US also encouraged maximum sentences, including the death penalty where applicable.Trump also urged Xi to increase the production of refined petroleum products to help stabilise global supply.New dialogue on ‘super intelligence’The two leaders agreed to use the term “super intelligence” rather than “artificial intelligence” for applicable emerging technologies.The US and China established the U.S.-China Super Intelligence Dialogue to exchange views on the risks and benefits linked to such technologies, with the next exchange scheduled for November 2026. They also agreed to establish a bilateral communication channel for incidents involving super intelligence.The two countries also agreed on a $30 billion reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement and to launch dialogue on AI under an eight-point consensus reached during Xi’s visit, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua.Global issues and strategic stabilityTrump and Xi discussed Russia, North Korea and Iran and agreed that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. They also agreed that no country or institution can be allowed to impose tolls on international waterways.The two leaders agreed to support each other as the respective hosts of the G20 and APEC, with both intending to attend each other’s summits.Trump also advocated trilateral arms control negotiations involving the United States, Russia and China.The leaders recalled that the United States and China had been allies during World War II and fought together in the war. Trump also highlighted the US forward military presence in the Indo-Pacific, which the White House said had contributed to generations of American prosperity.You use AI every day. articles.title: Giant cardboard replica of Weston-super-Mare pier created
articles.summary: The six-storey cardboard replica of Weston-super-Mare's Birnbeck Pier will stand alongside the real thing.
articles.body:
A giant cardboard replica of a historic pier has been created by 400 people using 2,000 boxes and 23.6 miles of sticky tape.

The six-storey-high structure, based on Weston-super-Mare's Birnbeck Pier, was due to be hauled into place alongside the real thing on Saturday.

Designed by visual artist Oliver Grossetête, who is known for creating large cardboard sculptures of architectural sites, has attracted volunteer helpers from all over the world.

"The spirit of the project is to make something together," said Grossetête. "I like cardboard because it is open to all people. For me, it's between architecture and a social project."

Paula Birtwistle, head of production at Weston-based arts organisation Super Culture, which is delivering the project, said the organisation was asked by North Somerset Council to think of a cultural response to the regeneration taking place at the pier.

"It has involved about 400 people so far, building the pieces, so that brings together a wide range of people," Birtwistle said.

"People have come from all over; lots of local people from the college, theatre students, people from the council, construction workers, sea cadets."

Birtwistle described the project as "bonkers" and said it showed "crazy ambition".

She said: "Hopefully people look at Weston and say, 'Wow there's really cool things going on there, they're punching above their weight'.

"I hope people who take part in it learn the impossible is possible.

"You can do anything with teamwork and if enough people do something, you can build something crazy."

Volunteer helpers have come from all over the world.

"Some people come back four or five times," Grossetête said.

"The spirit of the project is the mix of the population and it joins them together - old people, young people, the whole community."

One of those people is Deb Peretz who has come from the east coast of the United States.

"By chance I ran into them doing a build in New Zealand so I helped them there," she said.

"After that, if he was doing it somewhere I could get to, we would try and come.

"It's fun... it's always in some place we haven't been to before."

She said the community had brought the project together.

"It takes many hands to do one of these projects," she said.

A celebration will follow the installation of the structure later.

articles.title: Picture books to help children in Jersey understand dementia
articles.summary: Dementia Jersey and Every Child Our Future join forces to help children access the books.
articles.body:
Children across Jersey will be given access to books designed to help them understand dementia.

Every Child Our Future and Dementia Jersey have partnered up to provide picture books which explore dementia in "sensitive and age-appropriate ways". The books are set to be distributed among schools and community groups across the island.

CEO of Dementia Jersey Claudine Snape said dementia often affected families, including children.

"Having books that we can share with schools and recommend to families is a really valuable way of helping children understand dementia in a language that feels accessible and reassuring," she said.

The collection includes stories exploring memory loss, family relationships and the impact dementia can have on people's lives.

Among the titles are Why Does Grandad Forget? by Rebecca Oxtoby and Elmer and the Gift by David McKee.

A donation from the Lions Club of Jersey Swimarathon made production of the books possible.

Nicola Mackereth, programme manager at Every Child Our Future, said: "Books can give children a safe and gentle way into conversations about subjects that might otherwise be difficult to talk about."

Samares Primary School headteacher Jenny Posner welcomed the books.

She said they would give teachers "a valuable resource to support children's understanding of dementia and encourage sympathy".

articles.title: Athens explosion: At least two dead in blast near Acropolis in Plaka district
articles.summary: Local media report the property included a holiday rental, with US tourists and a UK national among the missing.
articles.body:
At least two people have died and four more are missing after an explosion destroyed a building housing a holiday rental property in the historic centre of Athens.

The blast happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis, with local media reporting the building housed a holiday rental.

An American man and woman have died, with two more US tourists missing, AFP news agency reported citing local officials. A Greek national and UK national who lived in the building are also said to be missing.

Pictures from the scene showed emergency service workers searching through rubble, with a gas leak the suspected cause of the blast.

The body of a woman was found on Saturday morning, with a Greek fire official later telling reporters the body of a man had also been found.

The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport, Reuters news agency reported citing local police.

Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said: "We are talking about an incredible disaster."

The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.

Local media reported people were injured by material scattered across nearby streets and some buildings needed to be evacuated.

Excavators and thermal imaging cameras have been used at the scene to search for survivors.

The explosion happened on a small road situated between two of Athens' most visited sites - the Acropolis and the Temple of Olympian Zeus.

A UK Foreign Office spokesperson said: "We are aware of a suspected explosion in Athens and are in touch with the local authorities."

articles.title: CNN barred from Trump’s Air Force One trip to Tennessee despite court order restoring White House access
articles.summary: CNN has been blocked from accompanying President Trump on Air Force One, despite a recent court order restoring their White House access, raising new concerns about media rights under the Trump administration.
articles.body: CNN has been blocked from travelling with President Donald Trump aboard Air Force One for his Saturday trip to Knoxville, Tennessee, just days after a federal judge ordered the administration to restore the network’s White House access.Two people familiar with the matter told The Washington Post that CNN was excluded from the presidential flight.CNN had been scheduled to accompany Trump to Tennessee, where he is due to attend a college football game. The network said on Friday that it was expected to travel with the president.The decision has also raised fresh questions over the future of the White House television pool, which briefly resumed its normal coverage on Friday.The pool is made up of rotating journalists who travel with the president and provide written and multimedia coverage to news organisations that may not have reporters present at every presidential event.Since the start of Trump’s second administration in 2025, the White House has determined which outlets participate in the pool. Previously, the White House Correspondents’ Association coordinated the rotation.Fresh dispute follows court orderCNN’s exclusion from Air Force One comes less than a week after Trump’s administration was ordered to restore White House access to CNN, MS Now and Politico.The three news organisations had challenged the administration’s decision to revoke their access, arguing that the move violated the First Amendment.The dispute began after the White House removed access for the outlets, citing their reporting about Trump’s presidency. Trump has repeatedly criticised what he calls the “fake news”.The decision triggered a protest from members of the White House press pool, who temporarily suspended their video coverage of Trump.In a joint statement issued on Monday, the White House television pool said the public had a “vital interest” in receiving accurate and independent information about the government.“No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting,” the pool said.The administration’s lawyers, meanwhile, argued in court that the restrictions were connected to national security concerns, citing media reports that involved “sensitive” and “classified” information.US District Judge Timothy Kelly subsequently ordered the Trump administration to restore White House access for CNN, MS Now and Politico.The outlets’ journalists attempted to enter the White House on Thursday morning following the ruling but were not admitted until around midday.Later that day, CNN’s editorial team and an MS Now reporter were prevented from covering a state dinner held to commemorate Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit.You use AI every day.
